Near-Optimal Constructive Bounds for \ell_{2} Prefix Discrepancy and Steinitz Problems via Affine Spectral Independence
Kunal Dutta
††thanks: University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Poland. kdutta@mimuw.edu.pl. Supported by the Polish NCN OPUS grant nr. 2023/51/B/ST6/02989.
Agastya Vibhuti Jha
††thanks: University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA. agastyajha@uchicago.edu.
Haotian Jiang
††thanks: University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA. jhtdavid@uchicago.edu.
A classical result of Steinitz from 1913 [53], answering an earlier question of Riemann and Lévy (e.g., [43]), states that for any norm \|\cdot\| in \mathbb{R}^{d} and any set of vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying \sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}=0, there exists an ordering \pi:[n]\rightarrow[n] such that every partial sum along this order is bounded by O(d), i.e., \big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}v_{\pi(i)}\big\|\leq O(d) for all t\in[n].
Steinitz’s bound is tight up to constants in general, but for the \ell_{2} norm \|\cdot\|_{2}, it has been conjectured that the best bound is O(\sqrt{d}).
Almost a century later, a breakthrough work of Banaszczyk [5] gave a bound of O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}) for the \ell_{2} Steinitz problem, matching the conjecture under the mild assumption that d\geq\Omega(\log n). Banaszczyk’s result is non-constructive, and the previous best algorithmic bound was O(\sqrt{d\log n}), due to Bansal and Garg [8].
In this work, we give an efficient algorithm that matches the conjectured O(\sqrt{d}) bound for the \ell_{2} Steinitz problem under the slightly worse, yet still polylogarithmic, condition of d\geq\Omega(\log^{7}n). As in prior work, our result extends to the harder problem of \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy.
We employ the framework of obtaining the desired ordering via a discrete Brownian motion, guided by a semidefinite program (SDP). To obtain our results, we use the new technique of “Decoupling via Affine Spectral Independence”, proposed by Bansal and Jiang [13] to achieve substantial progress on the Beck-Fiala and Komlós conjectures, together with a “Global Interval Tree” data structure that simultaneously controls the deviations for all prefixes.

1 Introduction
The Steinitz problem is a fundamental question in combinatorial discrepancy theory that studies how well one can control the discrepancy of partial sums of vectors under permutations.
Formally, given a norm \|\cdot\| and a set of vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying \|v_{i}\|\leq 1 for each i\in[n]11
1
Throughout, we use [n] to denote the set \{1,\cdots,n\}. and \sum_{i\in[n]}v_{i}=0, the Steinitz problem asks for the smallest number S(\|\cdot\|), depending only on the norm \|\cdot\|, such that there exists an ordering \pi:[n]\rightarrow[n] for which all partial sums along this ordering are at most S(\|\cdot\|), i.e., \max_{t\in[n]}\big\|\sum_{i\in[t]}v_{\pi(i)}\big\|\leq S(\|\cdot\|).
This was originally a question of Riemann and Lévy [43] from the early 1900s, and it has later found many surprising applications in areas such as graph theory [1], integer programming [25, 30, 31, 40], and scheduling [21, 50].
We refer readers to the surveys [35, 50, 22] for more details on the history and applications of the Steinitz problem.
A classical result of Steinitz [53] showed that S(\|\cdot\|)\leq 2d, regardless of the norm. Subsequently, this bound was improved to 1.5d in [21] and then further to slightly better than d [34, 3].
In particular, the proof by Grinberg and Sevastyanov in [34] uses a clever iterated rounding argument, which also implies an efficient algorithm for finding a good ordering \pi.
The above bound of O(d) is the best possible up to constants for general norms, e.g., S(\|\cdot\|_{1})\geq d/2. But for the \ell_{2} norm, the best lower bound is only S(\|\cdot\|_{2})\geq\Omega(\sqrt{d}) [24, 34]. While no o(d) bound is known for \ell_{2}, it was conjectured that \Theta(\sqrt{d}) should be the right answer.22
2
Note that one may assume d\leq n^{2}, as otherwise the trivial discrepancy bound of n already achieves the conjectured O(\sqrt{d}) bound. We make the assumption d\leq n^{2} throughout this work.
In breakthrough work, Banaszczyk [5] proved that S(\|\cdot\|_{2})\leq O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}), matching the conjectured bound up to constants under the mild assumption of d\geq\log n.
Unlike the O(d) bound above, Banaszczyk’s proof is non-constructive and does not give an efficient algorithm for finding a good ordering (we discuss more on algorithmic aspects of discrepancy theory in Section 1.3).
On the algorithmic front, [38] gave a constructive proof of O(\sqrt{d}\log^{2.5}n), and the previous best algorithmic bound was O(\sqrt{d\log n}) due to Bansal and Garg [8].
Unlike Banaszczyk’s result, these algorithmic bounds don’t match the conjectured bound for \ell_{2} Steinitz in any regime, and it is a natural open question to algorithmically attain Banaszczyk’s bound for this problem (e.g., see [6]).
Prefix Discrepancy.
A closely-related question is the \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy33
3
The prefix discrepancy problem is also referred to as the signed series problem in the literature. problem, introduced by Spencer [51]: given a sequence of vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with \|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], the goal is to find a coloring x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} so that the \ell_{2} norm of all partial signed sum is bounded by a number E(\|\cdot\|_{2}), i.e., \max_{t\in[n]}\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{t}\big\|_{2}\leq E(\|\cdot\|_{2}).
Variants of this prefix problem have been well-studied and they have many applications to online algorithms [41, 10, 9, 2], Tusnády’s problem [47], and flow time scheduling [15].
For \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy, Spencer [51] showed a bound that only depends on d. Using iterated rounding, Bárány and Grinberg [20] gave an algorithmic bound of 2d-1.
Similar to \ell_{2} Steinitz, it has been conjectured that the correct bound for E(\|\cdot\|_{2}) should be \Theta(\sqrt{d}).
The \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy problem is actually known to be harder than the Steinitz problem — Chobanyan [28] gave a reduction between the two problems which shows that S(\|\cdot\|_{2})\leq E(\|\cdot\|_{2}), and this reduction can be made algorithmic [38]. In fact, both the non-constructive bound of O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}) in [5] and the algorithmic bound of O(\sqrt{d\log n}) in [8] above were given for the harder \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy problem and then they used this reduction as a black box.
1.1 Our Results
Our main result is an improved algorithmic bound for \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy that matches the conjectured \Theta(\sqrt{d}) bound under the slightly worse, yet still polylogarithmic, condition of d\geq\log^{7}n (recall that in Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound, the condition was d\geq\log n).
Theorem 1.1.
(Algorithmic \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy)
Given v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with \|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], one can efficiently find x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that \big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\big\|_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\log^{7/4}n) for all prefix t\in[n]. In particular, the bound matches the conjectured \Theta(\sqrt{d}) when d\geq\log^{7}n.
Unlike the constructive bound in [8] that loses a multiplicative O(\sqrt{\log n}) factor, the bound in Theorem 1.1 (as well as the other results below) is only off from the conjectured bound by an additive factor, which is of lower order when d\geq\mathsf{polylog}(n).
While not stated explicitly, our bounds are also never worse than those in [8], as our algorithms are built on top of theirs.
Using the algorithmic reduction in [28, 38] as a black box, Theorem 1.1 also implies the same algorithmic improvement for the \ell_{2} Steinitz problem. This gets close to answering the question of algorithmically matching Banaszczyk’s bound for \ell_{2} Steinitz in [6].
Corollary 1.2 (Algorithmic \ell_{2} Steinitz).
Given vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that \sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}=0 and \|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], one can efficiently find a permutation \pi:[n]\rightarrow[n] such that \big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}v_{\pi(i)}\big\|_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\log^{7/4}n) for all prefix t\in[n]. This bound matches the conjectured \Theta(\sqrt{d}) bound when d\geq\log^{7}n.
It is an intriguing open question to improve the condition of d\geq\log^{7}n in Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 to get close to the condition of d\geq\log n in Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound [5].
We give such an improvement in the case where coordinates of the vectors v_{i} are “well-spread”, namely, each coordinate of every v_{i} has magnitude at most 1/\sqrt{d}.
Equivalently, one may scale the vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n} up by a \sqrt{d} factor and assume that each v_{i} satisfies \|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1.
Under this scaling, the conjectured bound becomes \Theta(d), where the lower bound is witnessed by a Hadamard matrix.
The previous best constructive bound for this setting was O(d\sqrt{\log n}) by Bansal and Garg [8].
Theorem 1.3.
(Algorithmic \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy)
Given v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with \|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], one can efficiently find x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that \big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\big\|_{2}\leq O(d+d^{3/4}\log n+d^{1/4}\log^{3/2}n) for all prefix t\in[n]. This matches the conjectured \Theta(d) bound when d\geq\log^{4}n.
1.2 Our Approach in a Nutshell
We view the given vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} as a matrix A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} whose jth column is v_{j}. Denote by A_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} its ith row.
Throughout, we use v(\ell) to denote the \ellth entry of a vector v and \log means logarithm to the base 2.
We always use i\in[d] to index rows of A, and j\in[n] for columns, and use \mathcal{P}\subseteq[n] to denote an arbitrary prefix whose discrepancy we will bound.
Similar to prior works, our algorithm starts with x_{0}=0^{n} and evolves a fractional coloring x_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n} using carefully chosen random tiny increments \Delta x_{t}.
As in [8], to handle all prefixes, our algorithm maintains a sliding window W_{t}\subseteq[n] containing the first 10d alive columns j for which x_{t}(j) has not yet reached \pm 1, and ensures that (1) \Delta x_{t} is supported only on W_{t}, and (2) the discrepancy update of the full sliding window is 0, i.e., \sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)\Delta x_{t}(j)=0 for every row i\in[d].
This guarantees that each prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n] only incurs non-zero discrepancy while \mathcal{P}\in W_{t}.
Roughly speaking, prior algorithms [7, 8, 14] choose the increment \Delta x_{t} to be O(1)-spectrally independent, which ensures that the discrepancy \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) for each prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n] and each row i\in[d] is O(d)-subgaussian.44
4
A mean-zero random vector \varphi\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is called \sigma^{2}-subgaussian, if for any unit test vector \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m},
it satisfies the Gaussian-type tail bound \Pr(|\langle\theta,\varphi\rangle|\geq t)\leq 2\exp(-t^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})).
This suffices for Bansal-Garg’s O(d\sqrt{\log n}) bound for \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy — subgaussianity ensures that each row prefix discrepancy |\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|\leq O(\sqrt{d\log n}) with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), which implies \|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq O(d\sqrt{\log n}) by taking a union bound over all rows i\in[d] and prefixes \mathcal{P}\in[n]. A similar argument can also recover55
5
The original proof of the \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound in [8] was done by analyzing the dynamics of d\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}^{2}, but a row-wise analysis already recovers their bound and is technically slightly simpler. Bansal-Garg’s bound for \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy, but we will focus on the \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} setting here for simplicity.
The main bottleneck for Bansal-Garg’s bound is that while each \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) is O(d)-subgaussian, they may have arbitrarily correlations, and this is why a row-wise analysis is needed to control \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) up to a 1/\mathsf{poly}(n) tail probability (and hence loses a O(\sqrt{\log n}) multiplicative factor) to union bound over all rows and prefixes.
To avoid this loss, we observe that if the \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) were mutually independent, standard concentration inequalities would
give an additive deviation, and recover Banaszczyk’s non-constructive O(d+\sqrt{d\log n}) bound.
Although it is clearly impossible to achieve full independence for \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i), we leverage the recent technique of “Decoupling via Affine Spectral Independence” in [13] to ensure that the change in prefix discrepancy \Delta\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) is affine spectrally independent — this weaker form of independence turns out to be sufficient for an additive \ell_{2} discrepancy bound on \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}, albeit with a worse additive term (than the fully independent case).
Nonetheless, the use of affine spectral independence posts a technical challenge — the independence degrades as one controls more rows/prefixes. Naively, at each time t, one needs to control d rows for each of the |W_{t}|=10d prefixes in the sliding window, but including all these \Theta(d^{2}) row-prefix pairs would result in too weak of an independence to even improve upon the Bansal-Garg bound.
To bypass this issue, we only enforce affine spectral independence for a carefully chosen set of o(d) prefixes in W_{t} called ASI-guarded prefixes.
To maintain this set of ASI-guarded prefixes dynamically and to bound the discrepancies of the remaining unguarded prefixes, we design a Global Interval Tree data structure to simultaneously control their additive deviations.
Roadmap.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows.
Some further related work will be discussed in Section 1.3. We then give an overview of our approach in Section 2. A formal presentation of our algorithmic framework, data structure, and meta analysis will appear in Section 3.
Then in Section 4, we prove our result for \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy in Theorem 1.3.
Finally, we prove our \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.1 in Section 5.
We will conclude and mention some open problems in Section 6.
Some missing details will be given in the appendix.
1.3 Further Related Work
Combinatorial Discrepancy.
Combinatorial discrepancy theory is a well-studied topic with many connections and applications to both mathematics and computer science, and we refer readers to the textbooks [26, 46, 27].
A classical question in combinatorial discrepancy is the following vector balancing problem: given a norm \|\cdot\| and vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the goal is to find a coloring x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} to minimize \mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}):=\min_{x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}v_{i}\big\|.
This question is easier than prefix discrepancy, as one only bounds the total signed sum.
For instance, for the \ell_{2} norm, a classical result of Bárány and Grinberg [20] shows that \mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|_{2}}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})\leq O(\sqrt{d}) when each \|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 and this bound is tight up to constants.
\ell_{\infty} Discrepancy and Algorithmic Aspects. While our focus here is on \ell_{2} discrepancy, we remark that \ell_{\infty} discrepancy is also very natural, and its study has led to many interesting techniques and developments in discrepancy theory.
A seminal result of Spencer [52] (and independently, Gluskin [33]) shows that if each \|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1 and d=n, then \mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|_{\infty}}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})\leq O(\sqrt{n}). This beats the O(\sqrt{n\log n}) bound for a random coloring, and is optimal up to constants.
When each \|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1, the long-standing Komlós conjecture, generalizing a seminal conjecture of Beck and Fiala [23], asserts that \mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|_{\infty}}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})\leq O(1).
For the Komlós problem, Spencer [52] gave an O(\log n) bound. This was improved to O(\sqrt{\log n}) by Banaszczyk [4]. His results for prefix discrepancy and Steinitz problems in [5] are crucially based on this earlier work.
While the above approaches for \ell_{\infty} discrepancy have become prominent in discrepancy theory, these methods were originally non-constructive and did not give an efficient algorithm for finding a good coloring. Following a breakthrough of Bansal [17], many elegant algorithms have been developed that matches these non-constructive bounds [16, 37, 44, 29, 49, 42, 32, 6, 7, 2, 14, 39, 48, 36, 12], leading to surprising applications in many different areas (e.g., see the excellent survey [18]). Interestingly, they also provide new insights into discrepancy theory and lately, building on top of these algorithmic developments, Bansal and Jiang [11, 13] gave an improved O((\log^{1/4}n)\cdot\mathsf{poly}(\log\log n)) bound for the Komlós problem and almost resolved the Beck-Fiala conjecture.
\ell_{\infty} Prefix Discrepancy. The \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy problem, where the objective is to bound \max_{t\in[n]}\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\|_{\infty}, is also well-studied.
When each \|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1, it was conjectured that the correct bound should be \Theta(\sqrt{d}).
Banaszczyk [5] gave a non-constructive bound of O(\sqrt{d\log n}), and this bound was later matched algorithmically in [8].
The case where each \|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 (i.e., the prefix version of Komlós problem) is more elusive. The best non-constructive bound is O(\sqrt{\log n}) [5], while the best algorithmic bound is only O(\log n) [2]. It was asked in [9] whether the Komlós conjecture generalizes to this prefix setting, i.e., whether the best bound is O(1), but there is no clear consensus on this question.
2 Overview of Our Approach
In this section, we give an overview of our approach. Our focus here will be on the \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.3, since it is technically simpler (than \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy) but already contains most of the ideas.
We start with the algorithmic framework that we will use throughout the paper.
Here we adopt the same notation as in Section 1.2.
2.1 Algorithmic Framework: SDP-Guided Walk with A Sliding Window
As in many previous discrepancy algorithms [8, 7, 14, 19, 11, 13], our algorithms start with x_{0}=0^{n}, and evolve a fractional coloring x_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n} over time using tiny random increments, until some final coloring in \{\pm 1\}^{n} is reached. The time t will range from 0 to n, and is updated in discrete increments of size dt. We will set dt=1/\mathsf{poly}(n) so that the algorithm runs in polynomial time, but it is useful to view dt as infinitesimally small.
Sliding Window and Coloring Update. At each time t, a column j\in[n] is alive if |x_{t}(j)|\leq 1-1/(2nd), and is called dead otherwise. Notice that rounding a dead column to either 1 or -1 incurs a negligible O(1/(nd)) discrepancy per column, and thus will be ignored henceforth.
Let W_{t}\subseteq[n] be the first 10d alive columns, which we will refer to as the sliding window.
The columns in W_{t} will be called active, and alive columns not contained in W_{t} are called dormant. The algorithm will only update the coloring x_{t}(j) for j\in W_{t}, and ensures that the discrepancy update of the whole sliding window is 0.
Specifically, at time t, the algorithm chooses a random vector u_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} satisfying \mathbb{E}[u_{t}]=0, \|u_{t}\|_{2}=1, x_{t}\perp u_{t}, and \sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for all rows i\in[d] (and various other properties that will be specified later).66
6
We sometimes abuse notation and also view u_{t} as a vector in \mathbb{R}^{n} with u_{t}(j)=0 for all j\notin W_{t}.
The coloring x_{t} is updated to x_{t+dt}=x_{t}+dx_{t} with
dx_{t}=u_{t}\sqrt{dt}.
Note that \|u_{t}\|_{2}=1 and x_{t}\perp u_{t} ensures that \|x_{t}\|_{2}^{2}=t for all t, so the process ends by t=n.
Also notice that \sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for all i\in[d] ensures that the sliding window incurs 0 discrepancy change, and thus any prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n] only incurs non-zero discrepancy when \mathcal{P}\in W_{t}.
Figure 1: Sliding window. Green dots denote alive columns, and red dots denote dead ones.
Choosing u_{t} via an SDP.
The power of this framework comes from the flexibility to choose u_{t} adaptively at each time t.
To do this, the algorithm computes a PSD matrix U_{t} by solving a semidefinite program (SDP), and samples u_{t} with U_{t} as the covariance matrix.
As this approach of sampling u_{t} via solving an SDP is already standard, to simplify the discussion here, we postpone the details of the SDP and how to sample u_{t} from U_{t} to Section 3.
2.2 Spectral Independence and the Bansal-Garg Bound
A useful property ensured by the SDP in prior algorithms is that u_{t} is O(1)-spectrally independent:
\displaystyle\mathsf{Cov}(u_{t})\preceq O(1)\cdot\mathsf{diag}(\mathsf{Cov}(u_{t})).
(\mathsf{SI})
Since \mathsf{Cov}(u_{t})=\mathbb{E}[u_{t}u_{t}^{\top}] for mean-zero u_{t}, this is equivalent to saying that for any vector a\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}},
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\langle a,u_{t}\rangle^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\sum_{j\in W_{t}}a(j)u_{t}(j)\big)^{2}\Big]\leq O(1)\cdot\sum_{j\in W_{t}}a(j)^{2}u_{t}(j)^{2},
(1)
which intuitively means that the coordinates of u_{t} is almost pairwise independent (up to a constant factor loss).
Surprisingly, this seemingly weak form of independence implies strong subgaussian-type concentration for discrepancy in the algorithmic framework above [7, 8]. In particular, if u_{t} is O(1)-spectrally independent for all time t, then for any test vector a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, its discrepancy change over any time period [t_{1},t_{2}] is essentially O(\|a\|_{2})-subgaussian, i.e.,
\displaystyle\Pr(|\langle a,x_{t_{2}}-x_{t_{1}}\rangle|\geq c\cdot\|a\|_{2})\leq\exp(-\Omega(c^{2})).
(2)
The Bansal-Garg Bound. The tail bound in (2) turns out to be sufficient to recover Bansal and Garg’s results in [8]. Here, we show their O(d\sqrt{\log n}) bound for \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy (their O(\sqrt{d\log n}) bound for \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy follows from a similar argument).
Recall that Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound is O(d+\sqrt{d\log n}) in the \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} setting.
Fix a prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n]. Denote A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\in[-1,1]^{\mathcal{P}} the row A_{i} restricted to the prefix \mathcal{P}, and denote \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=\langle A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}},x_{t}\rangle the discrepancy of row i for prefix \mathcal{P}. We will show that with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), |\varphi^{\mathcal{P}}_{n}(i)|\leq O(\sqrt{d\log n}) for all row i\in[d], which implies that \|\varphi^{\mathcal{P}}_{n}\|_{2}\leq O(d\sqrt{\log n}).
Taking a union bound over all prefixes \mathcal{P}\in[n] then gives the Bansal-Garg result.
To bound \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i), let t^{*} be the first time when column \mathcal{P} enters the sliding window, and let a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t^{*}}} be the vector A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}} restricted to that particular sliding window W_{t^{*}}. Clearly, we have \|a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{10d} as the sliding window only has 10d alive columns.
Since prefix \mathcal{P} does not incur any discrepancy before it enters the sliding window, we have \varphi_{t^{*}}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=0.
Note that only the coloring update of columns in W_{t^{*}} can contribute to \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} after time t^{*}, and thus \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=\langle a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}},x_{n}-x_{t^{*}}\rangle. Then using (2) with c=O(\sqrt{\log n}) for large enough constants and \|a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}) gives the desired bound
\Pr(|\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|\geq O(\sqrt{d\log n}))\leq\exp(-\Omega(c^{2}))=1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
Where Can We Improve?
The main reason for the O(\sqrt{\log n}) factor loss in the Bansal-Garg bound is the following. Although each \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) is O(d)-subgaussian, the different \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)’s may have arbitrary correlations, so they need to bound each \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) up to a tail probability of 1/\mathsf{poly}(n) to take a union bound over all rows i\in[d] and prefixes \mathcal{P}\in[n].
This row-wise analysis is generally the best possible without any additional control over the correlations among the \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)’s.
However, in an ideal scenario where the discrepancies of all rows \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) are evolving independently, standard concentration inequalities (e.g., see [54, Theorem 3.1.1]) give the following stronger tail bound for \|\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2} (than the row-wise analysis above) with an additive deviation:
\displaystyle\Pr\big(\|\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\geq O(\sqrt{d}(\sqrt{d}+c))\big)\leq\exp(-\Omega(c^{2})).
Taking c=O(\sqrt{\log n}) here allows for a union bound over all prefixes \mathcal{P}\in[n], and this would already recover Banaszczyk’s non-constructive O(d+\sqrt{d\log n}) result.
Of course, as the discrepancies \varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) of different rows i\in[d] are generated by the same dynamics dx_{t}, it is not realistic to assume that they are independent.
Nonetheless, this dependency among row discrepancies is exactly the issue encountered by Bansal and Jiang [11, 13] when studying the Beck-Fiala and Komlós conjectures. To bypass the issue and achieve substantial progress towards these long-standing conjectures, they devised a new technique to “decouple” the discrepancies of different rows using a new set of SDP constraints for u_{t} called affine spectral independence.
2.3 Affine Spectral Independence and ASI-Guarded Prefixes
The idea in [13] is to add a new set of affine spectral independence (ASI) constraints to the SDP to ensure that d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}=\varphi_{t+dt}^{\mathcal{P}}-\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} is \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-spectrally independent (see Section 3 for details), i.e.,
\displaystyle\mathsf{Cov}(d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})\preceq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot\mathsf{diag}(\mathsf{Cov}(d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})).
(\mathsf{ASI})
Similar to (1), this intuitively says that the discrepancy change d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) of different rows i\in[d] are almost pairwise independent up to a \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} factor, and we show that this weaker form of independence suffices for an additive bound.
In particular, we analyze the dynamics of d\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}^{2} as in [8],
d\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}^{2}=2\underbrace{\langle\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}},d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rangle}_{dL^{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}+\underbrace{\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}},d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rangle}_{dQ^{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}.
[8] already gave a bound for the quadratic term Q_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} matching Banaszczyk’s bound, using (
SI
) and a Freedman-type martingale analysis (see Section 3.3), and the main bottleneck there lies in controlling the linear term L_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}.
It turns out that the (
ASI
) property reduces the quadratic variation of L_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}, which allows us to show that with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),
\displaystyle\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq O(d+\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot d\log n}).
(3)
We defer the technical details to Section 4, but this essentially recovers Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound if the ASI factor \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} could be set to O(1) as in the spectral independence property (
SI
).
Controlling All Prefixes Blows Up the ASI Factor. Unfortunately, while we can indeed set \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=O(1) in (
ASI
) for a fixed prefix \mathcal{P}, a crucial issue arises when controlling multiple prefixes — the \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} factor suffers from the number of prefixes one needs to control simultaneously [13]. As the sliding window W_{t} has size 10d, naively satisfying (
ASI
) for all prefixes \mathcal{P}\in W_{t} would result in setting \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\Theta(d), for which the bound in (3) is no better than the Bansal-Garg bound.
To bypass this issue, we control a carefully chosen set of o(d) prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t} that we call ASI-guarded prefixes — this allows us to choose \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=|\mathcal{I}_{t}|=o(d) (and we will think of \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=|\mathcal{I}_{t}| henceforth), for which the bound in (3) improves upon Bansal-Garg.
However, this forces us to lose the (
ASI
) control over most prefixes (i.e., those that are not ASI-guarded, which we will refer to as unguarded prefixes), and this poses two further technical challenges:
(i)
As the sliding window W_{t} evolves over time, we need to update the set of o(d) many ASI-guarded prefixes dynamically.
(ii)
We need to control the discrepancies of all the 10d-o(d) unguarded prefixes. In particular, some of the previous ASI-guarded prefixes might become unguarded later on, and we can no longer rely on (3) to bound their discrepancies.
To get around these challenges, we design a data structure for maintaining the set of o(d) ASI-guarded prefixes that we call Global Interval Tree (and denoted as \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}).
2.4 Global Interval Tree: Controlling Unguarded Prefixes
In this subsection, we give an overview of the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure and discuss how it overcomes the above challenges (see Sections 3.2 and 3.3 for more details).
The Interval Representation. Denote \mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t} the set of \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=o(d) ASI-guarded prefixes that \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} maintains at each time t.
Note that \mathcal{I}_{t} naturally corresponds to a collection of consecutive intervals in [n], where each pair of adjacent ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} induces the interval (\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2}]:=\{\mathcal{P}_{1}+1,\mathcal{P}_{1}+2,\cdots,\mathcal{P}_{2}\}.
This collection of consecutive intervals essentially forms a partition (except for a final interval between \max\{\mathcal{I}_{t}\} and \max\{W_{t}\}) of the columns in [W_{t}], where we use [W_{t}]:=[\min\{W_{t}\},\max\{W_{t}\}] to denote the set of all columns, alive or dead, that lies inside the range of the current sliding window W_{t}. We refer to [W_{t}] as the complete sliding window, and note that W_{t} only contains all the alive columns in [W_{t}].
Figure 2: Partition of the complete sliding window [W_{t}] by ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}=\{\mathcal{P}_{1},\cdots,\mathcal{P}_{\ell}\}. Throughout, green dots denote alive columns, and red dots denote dead ones.
From this interval perspective, an equivalent task is to maintain a set of o(d) intervals that partition [W_{t}], which we abuse notation and also denote as \mathcal{I}_{t}.
As the sliding window W_{t} progresses over time, the set of intervals \mathcal{I}_{t} needs to be updated dynamically. For our purposes, we will perform two operations:
(1) add new intervals into \mathcal{I}_{t} when new columns enter [W_{t}], and (2) merge consecutive intervals in \mathcal{I}_{t} when their sizes, i.e., the number of alive columns they currently contain, become too small (and thus too expensive to maintain separately).77
7
Note that merging two consecutive intervals corresponds to unguarding the ASI-guarded prefix between them.
Adding and Merging Intervals. To describe these operations formally, we partition [n] into n/s base intervals of size s=\omega(1) each at time 0, and use \mathcal{B} to denote this collection of base intervals. We call a base interval I\in\mathcal{B} active at time t if I\subseteq[1,\max\{W_{t}\}] and I\cap W_{t}\neq\emptyset, i.e., when I contains at least one active column and no column in I is dormant.
At time 0, the initial sliding window W_{0} (as well as \mathcal{I}_{0}) contains the first 10d/s=o(d) base intervals.
We add a base interval I\in\mathcal{B} to \mathcal{I}_{t} whenever it becomes active, and we will only add base intervals to \mathcal{I}_{t} throughout.
An interval I\in\mathcal{I}_{t} is said to be small if its size is at most s/2.
Ideally, we would like to merge two consecutive intervals when both of them are small to ensure that there are no small intervals, but we will need to do this carefully — as we will see in the following discussion, merging an interval too many times may blow up the discrepancy of the prefixes it contains.
Two Conflicting Goals. Before describing our merging strategy, we first address the challenges mentioned towards the end of Section 2.3.
For challenge (i), the total number of intervals in \mathcal{I}_{t} must be o(d), which is equivalent to the average size of intervals in \mathcal{I}_{t} being \omega(1):
Goal (i): the average interval size in \mathcal{I}_{t} should be \omega(1).
To control the discrepancy of an unguarded prefix \mathcal{P}\in[W_{t}] as posted in challenge (ii), let I\in\mathcal{I}_{t} be the interval containing \mathcal{P}. The left endpoint of I is an ASI-guarded prefix which we will call the ASI-guard for \mathcal{P} at time t.
From this perspective, the discrepancy change for prefix \mathcal{P} can be decomposed as d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}, where d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} is the discrepancy change of its ASI-guard, and d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} is the discrepancy change of the (alive) columns between the ASI-guard and \mathcal{P}, which we will refer to as the error columns or the error set (see Figure 3 for an illustration).
Figure 3: ASI-guard for prefix \mathcal{P}, and the corresponding ASI and error components of d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}.
Roughly speaking, we will show (see Section 3.3 for details) that
the contribution from the ASI-guard part d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} can still be bounded as in (3), even though the ASI-guard for \mathcal{P} might change over time — thus as long as goal (i) is achieved, one has \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=|\mathcal{I}_{t}|=o(d) and this suffices for bounding the ASI-guard part \varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} better than the Bansal-Garg bound.
However, the discrepancy contribution of the error part d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} depends on the total number of columns that have ever been part of the error set for prefix \mathcal{P} at any time — it can be bounded by O(\sqrt{(\text{total \# of error columns})\cdot\log n}) using the Freedman-type martingale analysis in [8].
Note that the total number of error columns for prefix \mathcal{P} depends on how many times the interval I containing \mathcal{P} merges with the interval on its left (see Figure 4), and can be upper bounded by
(\text{total \# of times interval containing $\mathcal{P}$ merges})\cdot(s/2),
where recall that s/2 is the threshold size for a small interval. This leads to the following goal:
Goal (ii): for every prefix \mathcal{P}, the number of times the interval containing it merges is small.
Note that there is an obvious tension between the two goals above — avoiding small-sized intervals as in goal (i) naturally leads to substantial number of merges — but we will be able to achieve both goals using the strategy of merging via a global binary tree.
Figure 4: The error set grows after the interval containing \mathcal{P} merges with the previous interval.
Merging via a Global Binary Tree.
At time 0, we view the n/s base intervals as the leaves of a complete global binary tree \mathsf{Tree}_{0}, whose depth is \log(n/s)=O(\log n) (here we pretend that n/s is a power of 2 for simplicity).
At each time t, we maintain \mathsf{Tree}_{t} to be a subtree of \mathsf{Tree}_{0}, such that the leaf nodes of \mathsf{Tree}_{t} (restricted to [W_{t}]) correspond to all the intervals maintained in \mathcal{I}_{t}.
Roughly speaking, when two base intervals corresponding to sibling leaves in \mathsf{Tree}_{0} are both small, we will merge them into a single interval represented by their parent (and delete the two sibling leaves from \mathsf{Tree}_{0}).
More generally, our rule for merging intervals is the following:88
8
For technical reasons, the actual merging rule that we use is slightly more sophisticated (see Merging Rule 3.3).
Merging Rule: Whenever two consecutive intervals I_{1},I_{2}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} are both small at time t and they correspond to the two sibling children of a parent node I_{0}\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, we will merge I_{1} and I_{2} into an interval for I_{0}, and delete the two sibling children from \mathsf{Tree}_{t}.
We will show that this merging rule ensures that each node only merges at most O(\log n) times as the depth of \mathsf{Tree}_{0} is O(\log n), while at the same time, the average interval size is at least \Omega(s/\log n).
Setting s=\omega(1) properly then achieves our two goals above.
See Section 3.2 for details.
3 Preliminaries and Our Framework
In this section, we formally describe our algorithmic framework and the meta-analysis that we use to achieve our results.
We start with some notation.
Notation.
As in Section 1.2, we view the vectors v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} as a matrix A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} whose jth column is v_{j}, and use A_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} to denote its ith row.
For any W\subseteq[n], denote A_{i}(W)\in\mathbb{R}^{W} the row A_{i} restricted to columns in W; for a vector u\in\mathbb{R}^{W}, we sometimes abuse notation and view it as a vector in \mathbb{R}^{n} with all-zero coordinates in [n]\setminus W.
For any prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n], define A^{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\mathcal{P}} (resp. A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{P}}) as the matrix A (resp. row A_{i}) restricted to the columns in prefix \mathcal{P}.
We use \varphi for discrepancy, and \varphi^{\mathcal{P}}_{t} to denote the discrepancy vector for prefix \mathcal{P} at time t.
We always use i\in[d] to index rows of A, and j\in[n] to index its columns.
Throughout, v(\ell) is the \ellth entry of vector v and \log means logarithm to the base 2.
We write \lesssim (resp. \gtrsim) when the left-hand side is at most (resp. at least) a constant times the right-hand side.
We define a notion of intervals for subsets of [n].
An interval in [n] is a consecutive set of elements in [n]. For \ell,r\in[n] with \ell\leq r, we denote [\ell,r]:=\{\ell,\cdots,r\}, (\ell,r]:=\{\ell+1,\cdots,r\}, [\ell,r)=\{\ell,\cdots,r-1\} the closed, left-open, and right-open intervals with boundaries \ell and r.
For a set W\subseteq[n], we denote [W]:=[\min_{\ell\in W}\{\ell\},\max_{\ell\in W}\{\ell\}] the smallest interval containing W.
3.1 Algorithmic Framework: the SDP and Coloring Update
As described in Section 2.1, our algorithms find the desired coloring by evolving a fractional coloring x_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n}, with x_{0}=0^{n}, over time t that increments in tiny steps of size dt=1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
The fractional coloring x_{t} is updated as dx_{t}=u_{t}\sqrt{dt}, where u_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} is a carefully-chosen random unit vector supported on the sliding window W_{t}\subseteq[n] consisting of the first 10d alive columns,99
9
If there are less than 10d alive columns left, the sliding window W_{t} will contain all the remaining alive columns. This will happen after W_{t} hits the last column of the input matrix A, and in this case, we will not enforce the constraint \sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for any row i\in[d]. None of our analysis will be affected by this change of the size |W_{t}| at the end of the algorithm, and we will ignore this nuance throughout for simplicity.
so that |W_{t}|=10d. In particular, u_{t} will be chosen so that u_{t}\perp x_{t} and that the discrepancy change of the whole sliding window W_{t} is 0, i.e., \sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for all rows i\in[d].
As mentioned earlier, to choose u_{t} at each time t, our algorithms first computes a PSD matrix U_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}\times W_{t}} by solving an SDP, and then samples u_{t} with U_{t} as its covariance matrix (up to a constant scaling factor so that \|u_{t}\|_{2}=1).
We first describe this SDP below and then explain the intuition behind its constraints.
In prior works, this SDP has a few more parameters, but here we hard-code most of them to be constants to simplify our presentation.
3.1.1 The SDP and Its Feasibility
Let the factor \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=o(d) in (
ASI
) be a parameter, to be specified later (depending on the problem setting) but fixed throughout the algorithm.
As mentioned in Section 2.3, our algorithm maintains a set of at most \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} many ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t} using the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure.1010
10
The upper bound of |\mathcal{I}_{t}|\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} is to ensure that the SDP remains feasible at every time step t\geq 0. We discussed it briefly in Section 2.4 and will give more details in Section 3.2.
Based on the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure, at each time t, the algorithm chooses a subspace H_{t}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} with \dim(H_{t})\leq 0.1|W_{t}|\leq d, and a matrix E_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{(0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}|)\times W_{t}}. The rows of E_{t} exactly corresponds to the d rows of A restricted to the at most 0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}|/d\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} many ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}.
Consider the following SDP with matrix variable U\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}\times W_{t}} and parameter \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}.
\displaystyle U_{j,j}
\displaystyle\leq 1\quad
\displaystyle\text{for all }j\in W_{t},
(4a)
\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}(U)
\displaystyle\geq 0.1\cdot|W_{t}|,
(4b)
\displaystyle\langle U,A_{i}(W_{t})(A_{i}(W_{t}))^{\top}\rangle
\displaystyle=0\quad
\displaystyle\text{for all }1\leq i\leq d,
(4c)
\displaystyle\langle U,ww^{\top}\rangle
\displaystyle=0\quad
\displaystyle\text{for all }w\in H_{t},
(4d)
\displaystyle U
\displaystyle\preceq 10\cdot\operatorname{diag}(U),
(4e SI)
\displaystyle E_{t}UE_{t}^{\top}
\displaystyle\preceq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot\operatorname{diag}(E_{t}UE_{t}^{\top}),
(4f ASI)
\displaystyle U
\displaystyle\succeq 0.
(4g)
To understand SDP (4), consider a feasible solution U_{t} and a mean-zero random coloring update u_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} with U_{t}\propto\mathsf{Cov}(u_{t}) (up to a scaling factor).
We will show how to sample u_{t} given the PSD matrix U_{t} in Section 3.1.2. Here, we first explain what the SDP constraints imply for u_{t}.
Spreadness, Sliding Window, and Blocking Constraints.
The first four constraints are standard and easy to parse.
Constraints (4a) and (4b) ensures that the coloring update u_{t} “uniformly spreads out” among its coordinates, and avoids the trivial solution U=0.
Constraint (4c) is equivalent to \langle A_{i}(W_{t}),u_{t}\rangle=\sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0, and this ensures that the whole sliding window has 0 discrepancy update,1111
11
As mentioned in Footnote 9, this sliding window constraint will be dropped when W_{t} hits the last input vector. as mentioned earlier.
Constraint (4d) enforces that u_{t}\perp H_{t}, and this can be understood as blocking any vector w\in H_{t} so that its discrepancy does not change, i.e., \langle w,u_{t}\rangle=0. In particular, our algorithm always chooses x_{t}\in H_{t} to ensure that u_{t}\perp x_{t}, as promised earlier.
Spectral Independence and Affine Spectral Independence.
Corresponding to (
SI
), the spectral independence constraint (4e SI) guarantees that the random coloring update vector u_{t} is 10-spectrally independent. As explained in Section 2.2, this intuitively says that the coordinates of u_{t} is almost pairwise independent up to a constant factor.
Analogously, corresponding to (
ASI
), the affine spectral independence constraint (4f ASI)
guarantees that the discrepancy update d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} is \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-spectrally independent for all ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t}. Intuitively, this says that the coordinates of d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} are almost pairwise independent up to a \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} factor.
Note that the ASI factor \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} is proportional to the number of ASI-guarded prefixes in \mathcal{I}_{t}, and this dependency is shown to be unavoidable in general [13].
Using standard duality arguments, the feasibility of the SDP (4) was given in [13].
Fact 3.1 (SDP feasibility, [13]).
For any subspace H_{t}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} with \dim(H_{t})\leq 0.1|W_{t}| and matrix E_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{(0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}|)\times W_{t}}, the SDP (4) given by constraints (4a)-(4g) is feasible.
In fact, Fact 3.1 is a special case of Theorem A.4 from [13].
For completeness, we include the statement of Theorem A.4 from [13] and explain how it implies Fact 3.1 in Appendix A.
3.1.2 Sampling u_{t} from an SDP Solution
Once a feasible SDP solution U_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}\times W_{t}} is computed, the random coloring update vector u_{t} with \mathsf{Cov}(u_{t})\propto U_{t} can be sampled using the following standard approach (e.g., [13]).
In particular, let U_{t}=Q_{t}\Lambda_{t}Q_{t}^{\top} be its spectral decomposition. We choose
\displaystyle u_{t}:=(\text{Tr}(U_{t}))^{-1/2}\,U_{t}^{1/2}Q_{t}r_{t}=(\text{Tr}(U_{t}))^{-1/2}\,Q_{t}\Lambda_{t}^{1/2}r_{t},
(5)
where r_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} is a random vector with i.i.d. Rademacher random variables (taking values 1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each). Note that this ensures \mathbb{E}[u_{t}]=0, and also \|u_{t}\|_{2}=1 as
\displaystyle\|u_{t}\|_{2}^{2}=u_{t}^{\top}u_{t}=\frac{1}{\text{Tr}(U_{t})}r_{t}^{\top}\Lambda_{t}^{1/2}Q_{t}^{\top}Q_{t}\Lambda_{t}^{1/2}r_{t}=\frac{\text{Tr}(\Lambda_{t})}{\text{Tr}(U_{t})}=1.
3.2 Global Interval Tree
As mentioned in Section 3.1, the subspace H_{t} in the blocking constraint (4c) and the matrix E_{t} in the ASI constraint (4f ASI) are chosen based on the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure. In this section, we formally describe this data structure and state its properties that we will need.
To simplify our presentation here, we only describe the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure in the context of choosing the set of \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} many ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t}, corresponding to the rows of E_{t} in the ASI constraint (4f ASI). The choice of the subspace H_{t} for the blocking constraint (4c) requires a slight modification of the data structure given here. But as it is only needed for the proof of the \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy in Theorem 1.1, we will defer the details to Section 5.
In Section 3.2.1, we describe how \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} maintains and updates a partition of the complete sliding window [W_{t}] over time,
following the discussion from Section 2.4. Then, in Section 3.2.2 and Section 3.2.3, we prove the properties of \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} that we need.
3.2.1 Interval Representation and Operations
Recall from Section 2.4 that a set of ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t} can be equivalently viewed as
a collection of consecutive intervals that partition the complete sliding window [W_{t}].
Formally, \mathcal{I}_{t}=\{\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{\ell}\} splits [W_{t}] into consecutive intervals (\mathcal{P}_{j},\mathcal{P}_{j+1}], for j=0,\cdots,\ell-1 and \mathcal{P}_{0}:=\min\{W_{t}\},
along with a final interval (\mathcal{P}_{\ell},\max\{W_{t}\}] containing all columns in [W_{t}] larger than \mathcal{P}_{\ell} (see Figure 2).
We abuse notation and also use \mathcal{I}_{t} to denote the set of intervals in this partition of [W_{t}] (we will ignore the final interval (\mathcal{P}_{\ell},\max\{W_{t}\}]) when the context is clear.
The data structure maintains a set \mathcal{I}_{t} of at most \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} intervals that partitions [W_{t}] at each step.
Recall from Section 2.4 that as the sliding window W_{t} progresses, the data structure updates the intervals in \mathcal{I}_{t} via two operations: (1) add new intervals to \mathcal{I}_{t} containing newly activated columns in [W_{t}], or (2) merge consecutive intervals already in \mathcal{I}_{t} when their sizes (i.e., number of alive columns contained in them) become too small. We describe these operations formally below.
Initialization and Adding Intervals. Before the process starts, we partition [n] into n/s base intervals of size s=20\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}\,d\log n each, and use \mathcal{B} to denote this collection of base intervals.
At time 0, we initialize \mathcal{I}_{0} to be the first |W_{0}|/s=10d/s base intervals contained in W_{0}.
At each time t, a base interval I\in\mathcal{B} is called active if I\subseteq[1,\max\{W_{t}\}] and I\cap W_{t}\neq\emptyset (i.e., I contains at least one active column and no column in I is dormant).
We add a base interval I\in\mathcal{B} to \mathcal{I}_{t} whenever it becomes active, and we will only add base intervals to \mathcal{I}_{t} throughout.
Remark 3.2.
To ensure that columns in the final interval (\mathcal{P}_{t},\max\{W_{t}\}] are also controlled by the (4f ASI) constraint, the data structure always includes \max\{W_{t}\} as a “special” ASI-guarded prefix in \mathcal{I}_{t}. This ensures that the entire sliding window W_{t} also satisfies (4f ASI), and doesn’t affect the SDP feasibility.
To simplify our presentation, we will not make this extra ASI constraint explicit.
Merging via a Global Binary Tree.
The intervals in \mathcal{I}_{t} are merged
using a global binary tree, denoted by \mathsf{Tree}_{t}, that evolves over time.
Initially, \mathsf{Tree}_{0} is the complete binary tree of height \log(n/s) whose leaves correspond to all the base intervals \mathcal{B} (see Figure 5), and at each time t, tree \mathsf{Tree}_{t} is a sub-tree of \mathsf{Tree}_{0}.
Figure 5: \mathsf{Tree}_{0} is a complete binary tree whose leaves correspond to all base intervals \mathcal{B}.
Note that the leaves of \mathsf{Tree}_{0} correspond exactly to the first 10d/s base intervals \mathcal{I}_{0} when restricted to the sliding window W_{0}, and the rest of the leaves to base intervals not yet added to \mathcal{I}_{0}.
We maintain this property throughout — namely, we ensure
that the leaves of \mathsf{Tree}_{t} correspond either to intervals in \mathcal{I}_{t}, or to base intervals in \mathcal{B} that have not been added to \mathcal{I}_{t} yet.
We call the former type of leaves of \mathsf{Tree}_{t} active, and refer to them and the intervals in \mathcal{I}_{t} interchangeably.
For each active leaf v\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, we use \mathsf{size}(v) to denote the number of alive columns contained in the interval of \mathcal{I}_{t} corresponding to it, and call v small if \mathsf{size}(v)<s/2.
We refer to the two children of each node in \mathsf{Tree}_{t} as left and right child as they appear in Figure 5.
A leaf is called a left leaf (resp. right leaf) if it is the left (resp. right) child of its parent.
At any time t, we update \mathsf{Tree}_{t} by deleting certain active leaves (or equivalently, merging the corresponding interval in \mathcal{I}_{t} with one of its neighboring intervals).
Formally, our merging rule is the following.1212
12
It may seem natural to use the simple rule of merging two sibling leaves whenever they are both small, but this might create a sequence of \Theta(\log n) small left leaves (corresponding to a root-leaf path) if the sibling right leaf at the end of this sequence is not yet active. While this sequence of small left leaves is fine for the purpose of maintaining the ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}, it will create some technical issues when one tries to adapt the data structure to maintain the subspace H_{t} in Section 5. This is why we use the more sophisticated Merging Rule 3.3 instead.
Merging Rule 3.3 (Merging via global binary tree).
At any time t:
(i)
For any small left leaf v\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, delete it and merge its interval with the interval at the next active leaf (see Figure 6 for an illustration); do nothing if v is the last active leaf.1313
13
The case where an active small left leaf v is the last active leaf in \mathsf{Tree}_{t} will be ignored throughout our analysis. One can essentially view v as being deleted and merged with the next base interval when it becomes active. In particular, if the right sibling of v is also an active leaf, then also delete the right sibling and use their parent to represent the merged interval (see Figure 7).
(ii)
For any small right leaf v\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, if the left sibling of v has been deleted, then delete v and use its parent to represent its interval (see Figure 8 for an illustratoin).
Figure 6: When a left leaf becomes small, it is deleted and merged with the next active leaf.
Figure 7: When the right sibling of a small left leaf is also an active leaf, both leaves get deleted and the parent represents the merged interval.
Figure 8: When the left sibling of a small right leaf has been deleted, the small right left gets deleted and the parent represents its interval. Note that the parent is now a small left leaf, and it will be merged subsequently according to Merging Rule 3.3 (i), as illustrated in Figure 6.
Intuitively, one can view the merging by Merging Rule 3.3 as happening from left to right — as (i) describes, whenever a left active leaf becomes small, it immediately merges with the active interval on its right if there exists one.
The deletion in (ii) is mainly for the purpose of cleaning up \mathsf{Tree}_{t} when only a single right child of certain nodes in the tree survives.
3.2.2 Bounding the Number of Intervals
Merging Rule 3.3 allows us to lower bound the average size of active leaves in \mathsf{Tree}_{t}, and hence to upper bound their number, which is equal to the number of ASI-guarded prefixes |\mathcal{I}_{t}|.
Proposition 3.4 (Bounding the number of intervals).
At any time t, consider \mathsf{Tree}_{t} after Merging Rule 3.3 is completed. Then the average size of active leaves in \mathsf{Tree}_{t} is at least s/(2\log n). Consequently, the total number of active leaves is |\mathcal{I}_{t}|\leqslant(2|W_{t}|\log n)/s\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}.
Proof.
Note that there is no small left leaves in \mathsf{Tree}_{t} after Merging Rule 3.3 is completed (except for possibly the last active leaf, which we will ignore as mentioned in Footnote 13), as they all get merged by (i).
There might be many small right leaves in \mathsf{Tree}_{t}, but we will control their average sizes by charging them to certain non-small active left leaves as follows.
For each small right leaf v, consider its left sibling w, which must exist as otherwise v will be deleted by (ii).
Note that in the subtree of \mathsf{Tree}_{t} rooted at w (which may contain the single node w if it is an active leaf), there must exist an active non-small left leaf w^{\prime}, as otherwise the subtree rooted at w will get merged by (i). We will charge v to this non-small left leaf w^{\prime}.
Note that each small right leaf that gets charged to w^{\prime} is the sibling of one of its ancestors. As w^{\prime} can have <\log n ancestors (corresponding to the entire root-leaf path), <\log n small right leaves can be charged to each non-small left leaf w^{\prime}.
As w^{\prime} has size at least s/2, averaging over itself and all the <\log n small right leaves that are charged to it, the average sizes of active leaves in \mathsf{Tree}_{t} is at least s/(2\log n).
The upper bound on |\mathcal{I}_{t}| then follows immediately, as the intervals corresponding to the active leaves of \mathsf{Tree}_{t} form a partition of the sliding window W_{t}.
∎
3.2.3 Bounding the Error Sets for Prefixes
Recall from Section 2.4 (also see Section 3.3) that for any \mathcal{P}\in[W_{t}] that is not an ASI-guarded prefix in \mathcal{I}_{t}, we call it unguarded, and assign \mathcal{P}_{t}:=\max\{\mathcal{I}_{t}\cap[\mathcal{P}]\}, i.e., the maximum-indexed ASI-guarded prefix before \mathcal{P}, as its ASI-guard at time t (see Figure 3).
For an ASI-guarded prefix \mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t}, its ASI-guard at time t is defined to be itself.
Recall that the discrepancy change for prefix \mathcal{P} is decomposed as d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}, where d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} is the discrepancy change of its ASI-guard \mathcal{P}_{t}, and d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} is the that of the alive columns between the ASI-guard and \mathcal{P}.
We refer to this latter set the error columns for \mathcal{P} at time t.
The union of error columns for \mathcal{P} at all time steps is called its error set, and is formally defined below.
Definition 3.5 (Error set for \mathcal{P}).
The error set for \mathcal{P} up till time t, denoted as \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}_{t}, consists of all error columns for \mathcal{P} for all time steps t^{\prime}\leq t.
The error set for \mathcal{P} is defined as \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}:=\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}_{n}.
Note that the error set for \mathcal{P} depends on the outcomes of the randomness of the algorithm.
As discussed in Section 2.4, our bound on \varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} will depend on how large the error set for \mathcal{P} is.
Merging Rule 3.3 allows us to give the following upper bound on \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}.
Proposition 3.6 (Bounding the error set).
We always have |\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}|\leq(s/2)\log n=O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}\,d\log^{2}n).
Proof.
Our goal is to find a set |\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}}|<\log n of nodes in \mathsf{Tree}_{0} that may contribute to \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}, and show that the subtree rooted at each node in \mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}} can contribute at most s/2 to \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}.
To define the node set \mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}}, let v_{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathcal{B} be the leaf of \mathsf{Tree}_{0} (equivalently, base interval) that contains \mathcal{P}.
Consider the root-leaf path from the root \mathsf{root}_{0} of \mathsf{Tree}_{0} to v_{\mathcal{P}}.
Starting from \mathsf{root}_{0} and following along this root-leaf path, whenever a node v on the root-leaf path is the right child of its parent, we add the left sibling of v to \mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}} (see Figure 9 for an illustration).
As the depth of \mathsf{Tree}_{0}, and hence the length of the root-leaf path, is \log(n/s), we have \ell:=|\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}}|<(\log n)-1.
Denote the nodes in \mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}} as G_{\mathcal{P}}(1),\cdots,G_{\mathcal{P}}(\ell).
We abuse notation and also use G_{\mathcal{P}}(k) to denote the union of all leaf intervals in the subtree rooted at node G_{\mathcal{P}}(k).
Note that the intervals G_{\mathcal{P}}(1),\cdots,G_{\mathcal{P}}(\ell), together with the (partial) base interval v_{\mathcal{P}}\cap[\mathcal{P}], form a partition of [\mathcal{P}], and these are the only intervals that can contribute to \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}.
We bound their contributions below.
For each k\in[\ell], note that as long as the node G_{\mathcal{P}}(k) is not deleted, none of the intervals in its subtree will merge with the interval containing \mathcal{P}, and thus contribute no column to \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}.
Only when G_{\mathcal{P}}(k) becomes an active (left) leaf that is small can it merge with the interval containing \mathcal{P}, but in this case \mathsf{size}(G_{\mathcal{P}}(k))<s/2 and thus it contributes at most s/2 columns to \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}.
As the partial base interval v_{\mathcal{P}}\cap[\mathcal{P}] can contribute at most \mathsf{size}(v_{\mathcal{P}})\leq s columns to \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}, the size of \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}} is bounded by (s/2)\ell+s\leq(s/2)\log n, and this completes the proof.
∎
Figure 9: Decomposition of prefix \mathcal{P} based on its root-leaf path. Each node G_{\mathcal{P}}(k) added to \mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}} is the left sibling of a node on the root-leaf path that is the right child of its parent’s.
3.3 A Meta-Analysis
In this subsection, we give a meta-analysis of our algorithms that is common to the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3.
The specific instantiations of this meta-analysis and the detailed proofs in these two different settings will be given in the next two sections.
Fix an arbitrary prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n]. Our goal is to obtain a bound on the \ell_{2} norm of its discrepancy vector \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} (with entries \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=\langle A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}},x_{t}\rangle) with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), so that we can union bound over all prefixes.
Let t^{*} be the first time step when \mathcal{P}\in W_{t^{*}}.
As our algorithm ensures that the discrepancy update for the whole sliding window is 0 by SDP constraint (4d), \varphi_{t^{*}}^{\mathcal{P}}=0 and the discrepancy vector \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} is entirely due to the coloring update of the alive columns in W_{t^{*}} after time t^{*}.
In the following, we will condition on W_{t^{*}} and analyze the discrepancy update after t^{*}.
To keep our notation simple, we drop the superscript \mathcal{P} whenever the context is clear.
As mentioned in Section 2.3, we will analyze the dynamics of \|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2} given by
\displaystyle d\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert\varphi_{t+dt}\rVert_{2}^{2}-\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}=2\underbrace{\langle d\varphi_{t},\varphi_{t}\rangle}_{dL_{t}}+\underbrace{\langle d\varphi_{t},d\varphi_{t}\rangle}_{dQ_{t}},
(6)
and bound the processes L_{t} and Q_{t} (with increments dL_{t} and dQ_{t}) separately.
It turns out that just using spectral independence (4e SI), [8] already gave a bound on Q_{t} that matches Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound for the (more general) \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy setting.
Fact 3.7 (Q_{t} bound for \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy, [8]).
Consider the setting of Theorem 1.1. For the algorithm in Section 3.1, one has Q_{t}\leq O(d+\log n) with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
The above statement follows from Claim 27 in the proof of Theorem 24 of [8].
Bounding the Linear Term L_{t}.
The bottleneck for the analysis in [8], which results in their sub-optimal bound, is the linear term L_{t}. To apply Freedman’s inequality (see Fact 4.3) for the martingale L_{t}, they need to bound its quadratic variation \mathbb{E}_{t}[(dL_{t})^{2}], where \mathbb{E}_{t} takes the expectation conditional on the events on before time t. However, as they have no control over the vector d\varphi_{t}, they need to apply the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(dL_{t})^{2}\big]\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\big]\cdot\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}.
(7)
Note that (7) is quite wasteful when d\varphi_{t} has non-trivial randomness, and our key improvement over [8] comes from the randomness guaranteed by affine spectral independence (4f ASI) for the set of ASI-guarded prefixes in \mathcal{I}_{t}.
However, as the prefix \mathcal{P} may not be an ASI-guarded prefix, we don’t have almost pairwise independence for d\varphi_{t} and thus cannot directly improve over (7).
Instead, recall from Section 3.2.3 that we let \mathcal{P}_{t}:=\max\{\mathcal{I}_{t}\cap[\mathcal{P}]\} be the ASI-guard for prefix \mathcal{P} at time t, and decompose d\varphi_{t} as
\displaystyle d\varphi_{t}=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},
(8)
where d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}:=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}_{t}} is the discrepancy change of the ASI-guard \mathcal{P}_{t}, and d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} is the discrepancy change due to the error columns between \mathcal{P}_{t} and \mathcal{P} (see Section 3.2.3).
Correspondingly,
\displaystyle dL_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle+\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle=:dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}.
(9)
In our analysis, we will control the two terms dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} separately.
Roughly speaking, the ASI-guard part dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} can be bounded better than (7) because d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} always satisfies affine spectral independence (4f ASI), despite that the ASI-guard \mathcal{P}_{t} might change over time.
To control the error part dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}, note that the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure guarantees that there will be at most O(s\log n)=O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}\log^{2}n) error columns throughout all time steps t, which allows for a standard Freedman-type analysis.
We defer the details of how to bound these two parts of the linear term, depending on the specific problem assumptions, to subsequent sections.
4 \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2} Prefix Discrepancy
In this section, we prove Theorem 1.3, which is restated below for convenience.
See 1.3
We present our algorithm for Theorem 1.3 in Section 4.1 and its analysis in Section 4.2.
The proof of Theorem 1.3 will appear in Section 4.2.3.
4.1 Algorithm
Fix \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}:=100\sqrt{d}\log n and \tau:=\Theta(d+d^{3/4}\log n+d^{1/4}\log^{3/2}n) the target discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.3 (with a large enough constant). The algorithm follows the framework in Section 2.1 and it also uses the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure as described in Section 3.2 to maintain a set of at most \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t}.
At each time step t, the algorithm does the following.
1.
If there exists prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n] whose \lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2} exceeds the target \tau, it outputs \mathsf{ABORT}.
2.
Otherwise, it solves the SDP in (4), where H_{t}=\emptyset (i.e., there is no constraint of the form (4c)) and the matrix E_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\times W_{t}} contains a row A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}(W_{t}) (viewed as a vector in \mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} with coordinates 0 in W_{t}\setminus[\mathcal{P}]) for every ASI-guarded prefix \mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} and i\in[d].
By Proposition 3.4 and the setting of s=20\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log n in Section 3.2.2, the row dimension of E_{t} is
d|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\leq d\cdot\frac{2|W_{t}|\log n}{s}=\frac{2d|W_{t}|\log n}{20\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log n}=0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}|,
which satisfies the condition of Fact 3.1. Thus the SDP (4) is feasible at every time step t, and to bound the \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy of this algorithm and prove Theorem 1.3, it suffices to prove that the algorithm does not \mathsf{ABORT} with high probability.
4.2 Analysis
Fix any prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n]. We will show that, with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), the \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy \lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2} is at most \tau at every time step t. Since the algorithm runs for \mathsf{poly}(n) steps and there are n prefixes, a union bound across all time steps and prefixes completes the proof. In the following, we drop the superscript \mathcal{P} whenever it is clear from the context.
Road Map for the Analysis.
Following the meta-analysis in Section 3.3, at each time step t, we decompose the change of the squared \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy d\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2} as
d\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}=dQ_{t}+2(dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}).
Our goal will be to show that for any time t\in[0,n], with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),
\displaystyle Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3\ ,\quad L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6\ \text{ and }\ \ L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.
(10)
Once the above is shown, then by a union bound, one has \|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\tau^{2} for all time steps t, which implies that the algorithm doesn’t \mathsf{ABORT} with high probability.
For technical reasons, in our analysis, we will use the more stringent stopping condition (than the algorithm \mathsf{ABORT}s) based on (10). Namely, if any of the conditions in (10) is violated at any time t, we will freeze the process x_{t} and thus L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} and Q_{t} will have zero increment onward.
Stopping Condition 4.1.
We freeze the process x_{t} onward if any of the three conditions in (10), i.e., Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3, L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, and L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, is violated.
Note that the modified process given by Stopping Condition 4.1 violates (10) at some time step if and only if the unmodified process x_{t} does (at a possibly different time). Because of this equivalence, we will abuse notation and also refer to the modified process as x_{t}, and the quadratic and linear terms for the modified process as Q_{t}, L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}, and L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}.
For the modified process, we always have
\displaystyle\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\leq Q_{t}+L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/3+3(\tau^{2}/6+\tau^{2}/6)=\tau^{2}.
(11)
We will argue that with probability at most 1/\mathsf{poly}(n), the modified process violates (10), and we will do so by taking a union bound over the probability that each one of the three conditions in (10) gets violated.
As discussed in Section 3.3, the bound of Q_{t}\leq O(d^{2}+d\log n)\leq\tau^{2}/3 with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n) was already shown in [8] (see Fact 3.7).
In Section 4.2.1 and Section 4.2.2 below, we bound L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in Lemmas 4.2 and 4.4 respectively.
4.2.1 Bounding the ASI-Guard Part L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}
We first bound the ASI-guard term L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} in the following lemma.
Lemma 4.2 (Bounding the ASI-guard part, \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2}).
Consider the algorithm in Section 4.1. For any time t, with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),
L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.
Our proof relies on the following Freedman-type concentration inequality for super-martingales.
Fact 4.3 (Lemma 2.2 in [19]).
Let \{Z_{t}:t=0,1,\cdots\} be a sequence of random variables with increments \Delta Z_{t}:=Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}, such that Z_{0} is deterministic and \Delta Z_{t}\leq M for all t\geq 1.
If for all t\geq 1, we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\Delta Z_{t}]\leq-\delta\,\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[(\Delta Z_{t})^{2}]
(12)
holds with 0<\delta<1/M, where \mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\cdot] denotes \mathbb{E}[\cdot|Z_{1},\cdots,Z_{t-1}]. Then for all \xi\geq 0,
\Pr\big(Z_{t}-Z_{0}>\xi\big)\leq\exp(-\delta\xi).
Proof of Lemma 4.2.
Fix a time step t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}} exceeds \tau^{2}/6.
Recall that \varphi_{t} gets its first non-zero increment after the first time t^{\star} when the sliding window W_{t^{*}} contains \mathcal{P}. We may assume that t_{0}\geq t^{*}, as otherwise L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}} will be 0. Following [8], we denote \mathsf{Corr}=\mathsf{Corr}^{\mathcal{P}}:=W_{t^{*}}\cap[\mathcal{P}] the columns in W_{t^{*}} with index at most \mathcal{P}. Note that only columns in \mathsf{Corr} contribute non-zero discrepancy to \varphi_{t}.
Similar to the analysis in [8, 19, 13], we define the following regularized ASI-guard term
\displaystyle Y_{t}:=L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t}^{2}(j),
where we set \beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log n) for a sufficiently large constant.
Below, we will show that the increment dY_{t} satisfies condition (12) with a suitably chosen factor \delta. Here, we naturally map time steps t\in[0,n] to \{0,1,\cdots,n/dt\}.
If at any time t, the modified process x_{t} is frozen due to the condition (10) being violated prior to t, then L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}, and hence Y_{t}, must have been zero increment at time t. Thus the increment dY_{t}=0 trivially satisfies the condition (12) in Fact 4.3 for any \delta in this case.
In the other case where the modified process x_{t} has not been frozen up till time t. We will show that condition (12) in Fact 4.3 holds for some factor \delta>0 by computing the first and second moments of dY_{t} in the following.
Note that the increment of Y_{t} is
\displaystyle dY_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)^{2}\,dt.
In what follows, all expectations are conditioned on the filtration \mathcal{F}_{t}, or outcome of randomness, up to time t, and is denoted as \mathbb{E}_{t}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}].
Since \mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}]=0,
the first moment of dY_{t} is
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt.
(13)
The second moment of dY_{t} is bounded as
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dY_{t})^{2}]
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}dt
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]dt,
where we drop lower order terms with scale O((dt)^{3/2}), use (a+b)^{2}\leqslant 2a^{2}+2b^{2} in the first inequality, and use O(1)-spectral independence of u_{t} and that |x_{t}(j)|\leq 1 in the second. We bound the first term using affine spectral independence:
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}
\displaystyle\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}(i)^{2}\big]
\displaystyle=\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\Big(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)\Big)^{2}dt\lesssim\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]dt,
where the first step follows via \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-affine spectral independence of u_{t}, and the final step follows by O(1)-spectral independence of u_{t} and using |A_{i}(j)|\leq 1 for all i\in[d],j\in[n].
Combining, we get the following bound on the second moment of dY_{t},
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dY_{t})^{2}]\lesssim(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]\,dt\leq(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\tau^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]\,dt,
(14)
where we bound \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2} by \tau^{2} using (11).
Combining (13) and (14), we get condition (12) with
\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]\lesssim-\Big(\frac{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\tau^{2}\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}}\Big)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dY_{t})^{2}].
Then applying Freedman-type inequality (Fact 4.3) with deviation \xi=\tau^{2}/10, we obtain
\displaystyle\Pr(Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\xi)\leq\exp\Big(\frac{-\xi\,\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}+\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\tau^{2}}\Big).
(15)
To bound the exponent in (15), note that since \xi=\tau^{2}/10=\Omega(\sqrt{d}\log^{3}n) and \beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log n)=\Theta(\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n) (as \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=100\sqrt{d}\log n), the first term is bounded as (\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}})/\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}=\Omega(\log n).
The second term can be bounded as
\frac{\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\tau^{2}}=\frac{(\tau^{2}/10)\cdot\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log n)}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\tau^{2}}=\Theta(\log n).
Thus as long as the constant in \beta_{\mathsf{ASI}} is big enough and the constant in \xi is even (much) larger, the tail probability in (15) is at most 1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
Finally, to compare the target event of L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 with the event Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\xi in (15), note that
\displaystyle Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}
\displaystyle=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t_{0}}(j)^{2}-\Big(0-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t^{*}}(j)^{2}\Big)
\displaystyle=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}(x_{t_{0}}(j)^{2}-x_{t^{*}}(j)^{2})\ \geq\ L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}(10d)\ \geq\ L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\tau^{2}/15,
where we used that \beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}d=\Theta(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) and \tau^{2}=\Omega(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) (with a much larger constant).
Consequently, the event L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies that Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\tau^{2}/10, and thus,
\Pr\big(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6\big)\leq\Pr(Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\xi)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
Taking a union bound over all time steps t_{0} completes the proof of the lemma.
∎
4.2.2 Bounding the Error Part L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}
Next, we show how to bound the error term L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in the following lemma.
Lemma 4.4 (Bounding the error part, \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{2}).
Consider the algorithm in Section 4.1. With probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), we have
L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.
Proof of Lemma 4.4.
Fix t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}} exceeds \tau^{2}/6. Again we may assume that t_{0}\geq t^{*}, where t^{*} is the time step when prefix \mathcal{P} first enters the time window.
Recall from Section 3.2 that \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}} (resp. \mathsf{Error}_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}) is the set of columns that contribute to the error term L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} throughout the algorithm (resp. up till time t).
The set \mathsf{Error}_{t}, as a (random) function of t, is monotonically non-decreasing with several “jumps”, corresponding to the times when the interval containing \mathcal{P} merges in the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure.
We drop the superscript \mathcal{P} below.
We define the following regularized process for L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},
\displaystyle Z_{t}:=L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}x_{t}(j)^{2},
where \beta_{\mathsf{err}}:=\Theta(d\log n) for a large enough constant.
Note that whenever \mathsf{Error}_{t} has a “jump”,
Z_{t} decreases which is only helpful for us (and thus can be safely ignored henceforth).
Similar to the proof of Lemma 4.2, the condition (12) is trivially satisfied if the modified process was frozen prior to time t.
If the process was not frozen, the increment of Z_{t} is given by
\displaystyle dZ_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)^{2}dt.
Since both d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} and u_{t} are mean-zero, the first moment of dZ_{t} is:
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt.
(16)
The second moment can be bounded as
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(dZ_{t})^{2}\big]
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\Big(\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}\Big)^{2}
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}\big]+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\Big(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\Big)^{2}dt
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\|_{2}^{2}\big]\cdot\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\cdot\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt,
where in the last inequality, we apply Cauchy-Schwartz inequality for the first term, and for the second term, we use that the vector u_{t} is O(1)-spectrally independent and that each |x_{t}(j)|\leq 1. To bound \mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr] in the first term,
we note that d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}(i)=\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}. Then using that u_{t} is O(1)-spectrally independent and each |A_{i}(j)|\leq 1, we can bound
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\|_{2}^{2}\big]
