\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}(i))^{2}\big]\lesssim\sum_{i\in[d]}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}A_{i}(j)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt\leq d\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt.
Plugging this into the above gives the bound
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(dZ_{t})^{2}\big]\leq\big(d\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\big)\cdot\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt.
(17)
Combining (16) and (17) gives us condition (12) with
\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]\leq-\Big(\frac{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}}{\tau^{2}d+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}}\Big)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dZ_{t})^{2}].
Applying Freedman-type inequality (Fact 4.3) for deviation \xi=\tau^{2}/10, we get
\displaystyle\Pr(Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{*}}\geq\xi)\leq\exp\Big(\frac{-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\,\xi}{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}+\tau^{2}d}\Big)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n),
(18)
where the last inequality is obtained by using \beta_{\mathsf{err}}=\Theta(d\log n) (and thus (\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\xi)/(\tau^{2}d)=\Omega(\log n)), and that \xi=\tau^{2}/10=\Omega(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) (which implies that (\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\xi)/\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}=\Omega(d^{1/2}\log n)).
Finally, we note that the event L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies the event Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{*}}\geq\tau^{2}/10, because
\displaystyle Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{*}}
\displaystyle=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t_{0}}}\big(x_{t_{0}}(j)^{2}-x_{t^{*}}(j)^{2}\big)\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\cdot|\mathsf{Error}|
\displaystyle\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\cdot O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log^{2}n)=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-O(1)\cdot\frac{d^{2}\log^{3}n}{\sqrt{d}\log n}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\tau^{2}/15,
where the first inequality in the second line uses the error set bound of |\mathsf{Error}|\leq O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log^{2}n) in Proposition 3.6, the equality there uses our parameter setting \beta_{\mathsf{err}}=\Theta(d\log n) and \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=100\sqrt{d}\log n, and the final inequality uses \tau^{2}=\Omega(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) (with a large enough constant).
Combining everything, we get \Pr(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n) and this completes the proof.
∎
4.2.3 Putting Things Together
Now we are ready to put things together and prove Theorem 1.3.
Proof of Theorem 1.3.
We run the algorithm in Section 4.1, and we have already shown there that the SDP is always feasible.
Combining Fact 3.7, Lemma 4.2 and Lemma 4.4, the probability that any of the three (modified) processes Q_{t},L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} violates Stopping Condition 4.1 and (10) is at most 1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
As this stopping condition implies the target discrepancy bound \|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq\tau,
by taking a union bound over all time steps and prefixes \mathcal{P}, the algorithm never outputs \mathsf{ABORT} with probability at least 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
Finally, rounding the coloring of each dead column to \pm 1 incurs at most O(1) additive \ell_{2} discrepancy. This proves the theorem.
∎
5 \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} Prefix Discrepancy
In this section, we prove Theorem 1.1, which is restated below.
See 1.1
We give our algorithm for Theorem 1.1 in Section 5.1 and its analysis in Section 5.2.
The proof of Theorem 1.1 will appear in Section 5.2.3.
For our analysis, we also need to use an \ell_{\infty} bound on the prefix discrepancy \lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty} for every prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n], which will be given in Section 5.3.
5.1 Algorithm
Fix \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=100\sqrt{d}\,(\log n)^{-1/2}, and let \tau:=\Theta(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\log^{7/4}n) be the target discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.1 (with a large enough constant). Also set \lambda:=\Theta(\log^{3/2}n) to be our target \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound (see Lemma 5.2). Analogous to Algorithm 4.1, our algorithm here follows the framework in Sections 2.1 and 3.1, where it uses the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure from Section 3.2 to maintain a set of at most \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} ASI-guarded prefixes \mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t}.
The main difference from Section 4.1 is that our algorithm also uses a slightly modified version of \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}, denoted as \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}, to choose a subspace H_{t} to enforce the blocking constraints (4d). This is only for controlling the \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy, and we defer its detail to Section 5.3.
Formally, at each time step t, the algorithm does the following.
1.
If there exists \mathcal{P}\in[n], for which either \lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2} exceeds the target \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound \tau, or \lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty} exceeds the \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound \lambda, it outputs \mathsf{ABORT}.
2.
Otherwise, it solves the SDP in (4), where H_{t} is the subspace output by \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} and the matrix E_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\times W_{t}} contains a row A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}(W_{t}) for every ASI-guarded prefix \mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} and i\in[d].
Analogous to Algorithm 4.1, the row dimension of E_{t} is at most 0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}| (as we use the same parameters in \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}). By Proposition 5.8, the dimension of H_{t} is at most 0.1|W_{t}|. This satisfies the conditions of Fact 3.1 and hence SDP (3.1) is always feasible. In the remainder, we show that the algorithm does not \mathsf{ABORT} with high probability.
5.2 Analysis
Fix any prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n]. We will show that, with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), the \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy is bounded as \lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2}\leq\tau and the \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy is bounded as \lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda at any time step t. Since the algorithm runs for \mathsf{poly}(n) steps and there are n prefixes, a union bound across all time steps and prefixes completes the proof. In the following, we drop the superscript \mathcal{P} whenever it is clear from the context.
Road Map for the Analysis.
Following the meta-analysis in Section 3.3 and the analysis in Section 4.2, we decompose the
change of \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy d\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2} as,
d\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}=dQ_{t}+2(dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}).
Our goal will be to show for any time t\in[0,n], with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),
\displaystyle Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3\ ,\quad L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6\ ,\quad L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6\ \text{ and }\ \ \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda,
(19)
where the extra condition \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda is needed for controlling the ASI-guard part L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}.
Once the above is shown, then by a union bound, one has \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\tau^{2} and \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda for all time steps t, which implies that the algorithm doesn’t \mathsf{ABORT} with high probability. Analogous to Section 5.2, we use the following stopping condition for our analysis.
Stopping Condition 5.1.
We freeze x_{t} onward if any of the four conditions in (19), i.e. Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3, L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, and \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda is violated.
The bound for Q_{t}\leq O(d+\log n)\leq\tau^{2}/3 with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n) was already shown in [8] (see Fact 3.7).
In Section 5.2.1 and Section 5.2.2, we bound L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in Lemmas 5.3 and Lemma 5.4 respectively.
Finally, in Section 5.3, we will describe the modified data structure \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} that allows us to obtain the following bound on \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}.1414
14
We remark that in the current setting, there are algorithms (e.g., [2]) that achieve the better \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound of O(\log n). However, these algorithms and analysis are quite different from ours, and it is unclear how to achieve the same improvement for the framework that we use here.
Lemma 5.2 (\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound).
Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1 and the data structure in Section 5.3. For any time t, and every prefix \mathcal{P}\in[n], with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),
\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty}\leq O(\log^{3/2}n).
5.2.1 Bounding the ASI-Guard Part L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}
We first show a bound on the \mathsf{ASI}-guard term L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} in the following lemma.
Lemma 5.3 (Bounding the ASI-guard part, \ell_{2} to \ell_{2}).
Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1. For any time t, with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),
L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.
Our proof follows the same strategy as Lemmas 4.2 and 4.4, where we apply Freedman-type concentration for super-martingales.
Proof.
For a time step t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}} exceeds \tau^{2}/6.
We let \mathsf{Corr}=\mathsf{Corr}^{\mathcal{P}}:=W_{t^{\star}}\cap\mathcal{P} be the set of columns in W_{t^{\star}} with index at most \mathcal{P}, where t^{\star} is the first time the window W_{t^{\star}} contains \mathcal{P}. Recall from the proof of Lemma 4.2 that \varphi_{t} incurs a non-zero discrepancy only on columns in \mathsf{Corr}.
We define the corresponding regularized ASI-guard term as,
Y_{t}:=L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t}(j)^{2},
where we set \beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=O(1) for a sufficiently large constant. Below, we show that dY_{t} satisfies the conditions of Freedman-type concentration (Fact 4.3) for a suitably chosen \delta.
Like before, we map time steps t\in[0,n] to \{0,1,\ldots n/dt\}.
For time steps t, where x_{t} is frozen due to (19) being violated prior to t, then dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and dY_{t} equal 0 and trivially satisfy (12) in Fact
4.3 for any \delta. In the other case, we show that condition 12 in Fact 4.3 holds for an appropriate \delta>0, by computing the first and the second moment of dY_{t}. The increment of Y_{t} is,
dY_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)^{2}dt.
Conditioning on the filtration \mathcal{F}_{t} (or equivalently the outcome of randomness up to time t), the first moment of dY_{t} is
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}].
(20)
The second moment of dY_{t} is bounded as,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}^{2}]
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}dt
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt,
where we drop lower order terms with scale O((dt)^{3/2}), use (a+b)^{2}\leq 2a^{2}+2b^{2} in the first inequality, and use O(1)-spectral independence of u_{t} and that |x_{t}(j)|\leq 1 in the second inequality. We bound the first term using affine spectral independence.
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}
\displaystyle\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}(i)^{2}\bigr]
\displaystyle=\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}\lesssim\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt,
where the first step uses \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-affine spectral independence of u_{t}, and the final step uses that u_{t} is O(1)-spectral independence, \sum_{i\in[d]}A_{i}(j)^{2}\leq 1 for all j\in[n] and the \ell_{1}-\ell_{\infty} Hölder’s inequality.
Combining, we get the following bound on the second moment of dY_{t},
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}^{2}]\lesssim(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt\leq(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lambda^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt,
(21)
where we bound \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\leq\lambda^{2} by Lemma 5.2.
Combining (20) and (21), we get condition (12) with,
\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]\lesssim-\bigl(\frac{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\lambda^{2}\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}}\bigr)\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}^{2}].
Then applying Freedman-type inequality (Fact 4.3), with deviation \xi=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log^{4}n), we obtain
\displaystyle\Pr(Y_{t}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq\xi)\leq\exp(\frac{-\xi\,\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}+\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lambda^{2}}).
(22)
To bound the exponent in (22), note that since \xi=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log^{4}n)=\Theta(\sqrt{d}\log^{3.5}n) and \beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=O(1) (for sufficiently large constants), the first term is bounded as (\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}})/\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}=\Omega(\log n). The second term can be bounded as,
\frac{\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lambda^{2}}=\frac{\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log^{4}n)}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot O(\log^{3}n)}=\Theta(\log n).
Thus, the tail probability in (22) is at most 1/\mathsf{poly}(n) (provided that the constants in O(\cdot) for \beta_{\mathsf{ASI}} and \xi are sufficiently large). Finally, as in the proof of Lemma 4.2, the tail bound for Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq\xi implies a bound on the probability of our target event L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6. Note that as before,
Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}(10d).
As \tau^{2}=\Theta(d+\sqrt{d}\log^{3.5}n) (with a much larger constant), \tau^{2}/6\geq\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}(10d)+\xi. Consequently, the event L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies that Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq\xi and thus,
\Pr(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6)\leq\Pr(Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq\xi)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
Taking a union bound over all time steps t_{0} completes the proof of the lemma.
∎
5.2.2 Bounding the Error Part L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}
Next, we bound the error term L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in the following lemma.
Lemma 5.4 (Bounding the error part, \ell_{2} to \ell_{2}).
Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1. With probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), we have
L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.
Proof.
For t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}} exceeds \tau^{2}/6.
Analogous to the proof of Lemma 4.4, we define the sets \mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}} (which we denote by \mathsf{Error} for shorthand). The regularized process for L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}:
\displaystyle Z_{t}=L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}}x_{t}(j)^{2},
(23)
where \beta_{\mathsf{err}}=O(\log n).
Analogous to the proofs of Lemma 4.2, Lemma 4.4 and Lemma 5.3, we analyze the increments at a time t before the process has frozen.
The increment of dZ_{t} is given by,
\displaystyle dZ_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)^{2}.
(24)
Since d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} and u_{t} are mean-zero, the first moment of dZ_{t} is:
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}].
(25)
The second moment can be bounded as,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dZ_{t})^{2}]
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}\bigr)^{2}
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}]+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}dt
\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}]+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}],
where we ignore the terms of scale O(dt^{3/2}) as they are lower order and the second inequality follows via O(1)-spectral independence of u_{t}. We bound the first term as follows:
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}]
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}u_{t}(j)((W_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})^{\top}\varphi_{t})(j)\bigr)^{2}
\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[u_{t}(j)^{2}((W_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})^{\top}\varphi_{t})(j)^{2}\bigr]\leq\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}].
Combining we get,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}^{2}]\lesssim(\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]\ \lesssim(\tau^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}],
(26)
where the second inequality follows as the process has not frozen yet.
This satisfies the Condition (12) in Fact 4.3 as,
\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]\lesssim\bigl(\frac{-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\,\xi}{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}+\tau^{2}}\bigr)\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}^{2}].
Applying Freedman-type inequality for deviation \xi=\tau^{2}/10, we get
\Pr(Z_{t}-Z_{0}\geq\xi)\leq\exp(\frac{-\xi\,\beta_{\mathsf{err}}}{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}+\tau^{2}})=1/\mathsf{poly(n)},
where the last inequality is obtained by using that \beta_{\mathsf{err}}=O(\log n) and \xi=\tau^{2}/10, where \tau^{2}=O(d+\sqrt{d}\log^{7/2}n). This implies that (\xi\beta_{\mathsf{err}})/\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}=\Omega(d^{1/2}\log^{7/2}n/\log n) which is \Omega(\log n) and (\xi\beta_{\mathsf{err}}/\tau^{2})=\beta_{\mathsf{err}}/10=\Omega(\log n) provided the constant in \beta_{\mathsf{err}} is large enough.
Finally, similar to the proof of Lemma 4.4, the event L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies the event Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{\star}}\geq\tau^{2}/10. In particular, using \tau^{2}=\Theta(d+d^{1/2}\log^{7/2}n) for a large enough constant, we have
Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{\star}}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\cdot O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log^{2}n)=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-O(1)\cdot\frac{d\log^{3}n}{\sqrt{d}(\log n)^{-1/2}}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\tau^{2}/10.
Combining everything, we get \Pr(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n), and this completes the proof.
∎
5.2.3 Putting Things Together
Proof of Theorem 1.1.
Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1. There, we have already shown that the SDP at each step of the algorithm is feasible.
Combining Fact 3.7, Lemma 5.2, Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 5.4, the probability that any of the four conditions in (19) is violated is at most 1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
by taking a union bound over all time steps and prefixes \mathcal{P}, the algorithm never outputs \mathsf{ABORT} with probability at least 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
Finally, rounding the coloring of each dead column to \pm 1 incurs at most O(1) additive \ell_{2} discrepancy, and this completes the proof.
∎
5.3 Bounding \ell_{\infty} Prefix Discrepancy
In this section, we describe the data structure \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} and prove Lemma 5.2, restated below.
See 5.2
To bound the \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy, we will enforce a set of blocking constraints (corresponding to H_{t} in (4c)).
We describe these constraints and how it controls \|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{\infty} in Section 5.3.1.
Then in Section 5.3.2, we present the modified data structure \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} for maintaining these blocking constraints and analyze its properties. Finally, we prove Lemma 5.2 in Section 5.3.3.
5.3.1 Our Strategy
We follow the approach in [8] of bounding the prefix discrepancy |\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)| for each row i\in[d].
Recall that \varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) only incurs non-zero discrepancy when \mathcal{P}\in W_{t} (due to constraint (4d)).
To control its discrepancy while \mathcal{P}\in W_{t}, we impose a set of blocking constraints (i.e., H_{t}\neq\emptyset in (4c)).
We fix an arbitrary row i\in[d] and describe the blocking constraints for row i below.
At each time step t, we maintain a subset \mathcal{J}_{i,t}\subseteq W_{t} and include the prefix A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}^{\prime}} of row i into the subspace H_{t} for each \mathcal{P}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{J}_{i,t}, i.e., we ensure that d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P^{\prime}}}(i)=0 for any \mathcal{P}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{J}_{i,t}.
We require \sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,t}|\leq 0.1|W_{t}| to ensure that \dim(H_{t})\leq 0.1|W_{t}|, as needed in Fact 3.1.
The data structure \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} that maintains the sets \{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]} will be given in Section 5.3.2. Here, we show to bound |\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|, and we drop the superscript \mathcal{P} below when the context is clear.
Bad Columns for \mathcal{P}, and Bounding |\varphi_{t}(i)|.
Borrowing terminology from Section 3.2, we call \mathcal{J}_{i,t} the blocking-guarded prefixes for row i, and call the remaining prefixes unguarded for row i.
For each unguarded prefix \mathcal{P}\in[W_{t}] for row i, we call \max\{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\cap[\mathcal{P}]\}, i.e., the maximum-indexed blocking-guarded prefix prior to \mathcal{P}, its blocking-guard for row i. The alive columns between the blocking-guard and \mathcal{P} will be called bad columns. Analogous to Definition 3.5, we define the following notation of bad set for prefix \mathcal{P} in row i.
Definition 5.5 (Bad set for \mathcal{P} in row i).
The bad set for prefix \mathcal{P} in row i up to time t, denoted as \mathsf{Bad}_{i,t}^{\mathcal{P}}, is the union of all bad columns for \mathcal{P} at all time steps t^{\prime}\leq t. The bad set for \mathcal{P} is defined as \mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i}:=\mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i,n}.
Note that the blocking-guard of prefix \mathcal{P} incurs zero discrepancy change at time t, and thus
d\varphi_{t}(i)=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{bad}}(i),
where d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{bad}}(i) is the discrepancy change due to the bad columns for row i at time t (see Figure 10).
Figure 10: The blocking-guard for prefix \mathcal{P} in row i. The discrepancy change d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{bad}}(i) is entirely due to the set of bad columns.
It turns out that the contribution of the bad columns depends on their \ell_{2}^{2} mass, where we define the \ell_{2}^{2} mass of a set S\subseteq[n] in row i to be \|A_{i}(S)\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j\in S}A_{i}(j)^{2}.
In particular, [8, Theorem 1] gives the bound |\varphi_{t}(i)|\leq O(\sqrt{\|A_{i}(\mathsf{Bad}_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\log n}) with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n).
Therefore, to obtain the result in Lemma 5.2, we need to bound \|A_{i}(\mathsf{Bad}_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\leq O(\log^{2}n). We will show how \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} achieves this condition in Section 5.3.2.
5.3.2 Modified Global Interval Tree
In this section, we describe the data structure \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} for maintaining the blocking constraints \{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]}.
The idea is similar to \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}, but we include a full description here for completeness.
Similar to the interval representation in Section 3.2, the set of blocking-guarded prefixes \mathcal{J}_{i,t} (for row i) corresponds naturally to consecutive intervals that partition [W_{t}]. We abuse notation and also use \mathcal{J}_{i,t} to denote the set of intervals in this partition.
\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} maintains these intervals \{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]} (that satisfy \sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,t}|\leq 0.1|W_{t}|) by adding and merging (small) intervals as before.
Initialization and Adding Intervals. Before the process starts, for each row i\in[d], we split [n] into a collection \mathcal{B}_{i,0} of base intervals, each with \ell_{2}-squared mass s_{0}=20\log n.
Then, \mathcal{J}_{i,0} will be the set of all base intervals that are completely contained in the first 10d columns.1515
15
We do not need an extra constraint at the end of the window as in Remark 3.2, since the entire time window W_{t} is blocked at each time step t due to (4c).
Note that the total \ell_{2}^{2} mass of W_{0} over all d rows is at most |W_{0}| (as each column has \ell_{2} norm at most 1), we have \sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,0}|\leq 0.1|W_{0}|.
As before, the data structure adds a base interval in \mathcal{B}_{i,0} to \mathcal{J}_{i,t} whenever it becomes active, i.e., it contains an active column and no dormant column.
Merging Intervals.
Analogous to Section 3.2, the intervals in \mathcal{J}_{i,t} are merged using a global binary tree \mathsf{Tree}_{i,t}. Initially, \mathsf{Tree}_{i,0} is the complete binary tree of height O(\log n) whose leaves correspond to all the base intervals \mathcal{B}_{i,0}, and at each time t, \mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} is a subtree of \mathsf{Tree}_{i,0}. As before, the active leaves of \mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} correspond to intervals in \mathcal{J}_{i,t}.
As before, sibling leaves of \mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} are merged carefully when they become small, defined as follows. The \ell_{2}^{2} size of an interval I in row i at time t is defined to be the \ell_{2}^{2} mass (in row i) of the alive columns contained in I at time t.
We call an interval small if its \ell_{2}^{2} size is \leq s_{0}/2=10\log n at time t.
Analogous to Merging Rule 3.3, \mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} is updated via the following merging rule.
Merging Rule 5.6 (Merging via \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}).
At any time t,
1.
For any small left leaf v\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, delete it and merge its interval with the interval at the next leaf; In particular, if the right sibling of v is also a leaf, then also delete the right siblind and use their parent to represent the merged interval.
2.
For any small right leaf v\in\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t}, if their left sibling of v has been deleted, then delete v and use its parent to represent its interval.
We end this subsubsection by proving the correctness of \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}. In Proposition 5.7, we bound the number of intervals in \{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]} and in Proposition 5.8, we show that \mathsf{Bad}_{i}^{\mathcal{P}} has small \ell_{2}^{2} mass.
Proposition 5.7 (Number of blocking constraints).
At any time t, consider \mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} after Merging Rule 5.6 is completed. Then the average \ell_{2}^{2} size of active leaves in \mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} is at least s_{0}/(2\log n)=10. Consequently, the total number of blocking constraints is \big|\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\big|\leq 0.1|W_{t}|.
Proof.
The proof is essentially the same as the proof of Proposition 3.4.
As before, there is no small left leaf. By the same charging argument there (that charges <\log n small right leaves to any active non-small left leaf), the average \ell_{2}^{2} size of the active leaves (or intervals in \mathcal{J}_{i,t}) is at least s_{0}/(2\log n)=10. The second statement in the proposition then follows immediately, by noting that the total \ell_{2}^{2} size of the time window W_{t} is at most |W_{t}|.
∎
Next we show how to bound the \ell_{2}^{2} mass of the bad set for \mathcal{P} in row i.
Proposition 5.8 (Bounding the bad set).
The \ell_{2}^{2} mass of \mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i} is at most (s/2)\log n=O(\log^{2}n).
Proof.
This proof is essentially the same as the proof of Proposition 3.6, by decomposing the prefix \mathcal{P} into a union of <\log n subtrees (for row i), and show that each subtree contributes at most s/2 to the \ell_{2}^{2} mass of \mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i}. We omit the details.
∎
5.3.3 Proof of Lemma 5.2
Now we are ready to complete the proof of Lemma 5.2.
Proof of Lemma 5.2.
Fix a prefix \mathcal{P} and a row i\in[d].
Proposition 5.7 ensures that \sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,t}|\leq 0.1|W_{t}| at each time t, so that the condition of Fact 3.1 is met and the algorithm is feasible.
By Proposition 5.8, the \ell_{2}^{2} mass of \mathsf{Bad}_{i}^{\mathcal{P}} is at most O(\log^{2}n).
Then by [8, Theorem 1], with probability 1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), all time t one has
|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|\leq O\Big(\sqrt{\big\|A_{i}(\mathsf{Bad}_{i}^{\mathcal{P}})\big\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\log n}\Big)\leq O(\log^{3/2}n).
Taking a union bound over all prefixes \mathcal{P}\in[n] and rows i\in[d] completes the proof.
∎
6 Concluding Remarks
Our constructive bounds for \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy and Steinitz problems match the conjectured bounds when d\geq\mathsf{polylog}(n), where the \mathsf{polylog} factors are larger than those in Banaszczyk’s non-constructive results (where he only requires d\geq\log n).
Below, we briefly explain the several reasons for this loss in our current analysis and mention some related open problems.
(a)
First, in the \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure, we lower bound the average interval size by \Omega(s/\log n) (even though the base intervals have size s), which results in an extra \log n factor in the number of intervals we need to maintain; we also upper bound the size of the error set by O(s\log n). Both these \log n factors are due to the global binary tree having depth \Theta(\log n). Nonetheless, as the sliding window has size |W_{t}|=O(d), it may be possible to reduce these factors to \log d if we could maintain a binary tree structure within W_{t}.
(b)
Second, as we are controlling \gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{d}) many ASI-guarded prefixes simultaneously, this leads to an extra \widetilde{\Theta}(d^{1/4}) factor in the additive term (e.g., see (3)).
Getting rid of this factor would require attaining O(1)-affine spectral independence (or equivalently, satisfying (4f ASI) for only O(1) prefixes), and it is unclear how to achieve this.
(c)
Third, we used the \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound of O(\log^{3/2}n) in Lemma 5.2.
The extra \sqrt{\log n} loss (from the current best constructive bound of O(\log n) in [2]) is due to the \Theta(\log n) depth of \mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}, and it may be possible to replace it by a \log d factor as mentioned in (a). Alternatively, it would be interesting to see if the (rather) different ideas in [2] could be combined with our algorithmic framework to achieve a O(\log n) bound directly.
We now mention some open problems related to prefix discrepancy below.
Matching Banaszczyk’s Bound Algorithmically. It is an intriguing open question to match Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound for \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy.
Question 6.1 (Matching Banaszczyk’s bound for \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy).
Given vectors v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with \lVert v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], does there exist an efficient algorithm that finds x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that \lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}) for all prefix t\in[n]?
Similarly, for the \ell_{2} to \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy (i.e., the prefix version of Komlós problem), it is widely open how to attain Banaszczyk’s O(\sqrt{\log n}) bound algorithmically. As mentioned earlier, the current best algorithmic bound is O(\log n) [2].
Question 6.2 (Matching Banaszczyk’s bound for prefix Komlós).
Given v_{1},v_{2},\ldots v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with \lVert v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], does there exist an efficient algorithm that can find x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that \lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq O(\sqrt{\log n}) for all prefix t\in[n]?
More generally, any algorithm that can find a random coloring x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that every prefix discrepancy vector is O(1)-subgaussian can attain both bounds above (in fact, this prefix O(1)-subgaussian property is equivalent to Banaszczyk’s result in [5]).
Currently, the best algorithm can only achieve O(\log n)-subgaussianity for every prefix discrepancy [2].
Beating Banaszczyk’s Bound for Prefix Discrepancy. For some time, one of the central goals of algorithmic discrepancy has been to match Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound algorithmically. But recently, [11, 13] were able to go beyond and substantially improve upon Banaszczyk’s result for the Beck-Fiala and Komlós problems.
It would be very interesting (and significant) to improve upon Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bounds for prefix discrepancy problems.
Question 6.3 (Beating Banaszczyk’s bound for \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} prefix discrepancy).
Given v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with \lVert v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], does there exist x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} with \lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d})+o(\sqrt{\log n})?
Similarly, it is an open question to beat Banaszczyk’s O(\sqrt{d\log n}) bound for the \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy problem. Interestingly, unlike the \ell_{2} to \ell_{2} setting, an algorithm matching Banaszczyk’s bound in this setting is known [8].
Question 6.4 (Beating Banaszczyk’s bound for \ell_{\infty} to \ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy).
Given v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with \lVert v_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1 for each i\in[n], does there exist x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} with \lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq o(\sqrt{d\log n})?
Another closely related question is Tusnády’s problem, which asks for the combinatorial discrepancy of all axis-parallel rectangles for an arbitrary set of n points in [0,1]^{d}.
For this problem, the current best lower bound is \Omega(\log^{d-1}n) [45], while the current best non-constructive bound (which crucially relies on Banaszczyk’s result) is O(\log^{d-1/2}n) [47], and the current best constructive bound is O(\log^{d}n) [8].
It would be quite interesting to improve any of these results.
Appendix A SDP Feasibility
In this subsection, we give the statement of the SDP feasibility theorem in [13, Theorem A.4] and explain how Fact 3.1 follows from it.
Theorem A.1 (Theorem A.4 of [13]).
Let W\subset\mathbb{R}^{h} be a subspace with dimension \mathrm{dim}(W)=\delta h, and E_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{s}h\times h} for all s\in[q] be a set of matrices with r_{s}\geq 1. Then, for any 0\leq\kappa,\eta,\eta_{s}<1, where s\in[q], such that \eta+\kappa+\sum_{s=1}^{q}\eta_{s}\leq 1-\delta, there is an h\times h PSD matrix U satisfying:
1.
U_{j,j}\leq 1 for all j\in[h],
2.
\mathrm{Tr}(U)\geq\kappa h,
3.
\langle ww^{\top},U\rangle for all w\in W,
4.
U\preceq\frac{1}{\eta}\mathsf{diag}(U), and
5.
E_{s}UE_{s}^{\top}\preceq\frac{r_{s}}{\eta_{s}}\mathsf{diag}(E_{s}UE_{s}^{\top}) for all s\in[q].
Furthermore, such a PSD matrix U can be computed by solving a semidefinite program (SDP).
To obtain Fact 3.1 from Theorem A.1, we set the parameters in Theorem A.1 for our SDP (4) as follows.
We set \kappa=0.1 corresponding to the trace condition in (4b).
Blocking Constraints. The subspace W in Theorem A.1 will contain the subspace H_{t} for the blocking constraints in (4c), which has \dim(H_{t})\leq 0.1|W_{t}|, as well as the d rows of the sliding window W_{t} provided |W_{t}|=10d (as mentioned in Footnote 11, if |W_{t}|<10d, the constraint (4d) will be dropped).
This corresponds to setting \delta to be at most 0.2 in Theorem A.1.
SI Constraint. The SI constraint (4e SI) corresponds to setting \eta=0.1 in Theorem A.1.
ASI Constraint. The constraint (4f ASI) corresponds to setting q=1 and \eta_{1}=0.1 in Theorem A.1, as the ratio between the row and column dimensions of E_{t} is r_{1}=0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}.
The parameter setting above clearly satisfies \kappa+\delta+\eta+\eta_{1}<1, and thus Theorem A.1 implies the feasibility of our SDP (4) and hence Fact 3.1.

Instructions for reporting errors
We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
methods listed below:
Click the "Report Issue" (
) button, located in the page header.
Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
all.
Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
We gratefully acknowledge support from
our major funders,
member institutions, ,
and all contributors.
